newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Courtaulds sees viscose margin up.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Courtaulds sees viscose margin up.

text.p: British chemical group Courtaulds Plc said margins in the viscose business have just begun to pick up, but it expects the full benefits only to come through by April.
In a telephone interview with Reuters, chief executive Gordon Campbell said the margin increase followed a price rise of about five percent.
"But it won't really work through until the next quarter," said Campbell, adding that price negotiations with customers were responsible for the delay.
His comment follows Courtauld's earlier announcement that it would cut its European viscose capacity by 20 percent in a bid to fight general oversupply.
Courtaulds, whose European viscose operations are located in Britain and Germany, will reduce capacity at its Grimsby plant in northern England by 25,000 tonnes per year from 55,000.

Campbell said he could not rule out further restructuring measures. "It's obviously what we think is necessary at this point in time, but I cannot give any guarantee whether more is required," he said. "It depends on whether the market will continue to recover.

Courtaulds said earlier that with the exception of the viscose fibres, trading in all its business had improved. Campbell said he was particularly pleased with the performance of the coatings business.
But he added that profit growth in the fibres and chemicals business was held back by the weak yen compared to the dollar, which hurts Tencel exports from the U.S. to the big Japanese market.
Tencel is a relatively new man-made fibre derived from woodpulp. Courtaulds is the only firm to sell Tencel and has aimed supplies at the upper end of the textiles market.
Campbell said the pound's persistent strength versus the dollar was hurting results, but he added it was impossible to quantify the negative impact stemming from adverse currency movements.

He said overall group pre-tax and operating profit for the year to March 31 would show an improvement when taking into account a loss of 15 million stg in operating profit due to disposals of non-core assets.
Pre-tax profit for the year to March 31, 1996 was 131.5 million pounds. Up until today analysts' forecasts for the current financial year ranged from 134 to 140 million pounds, Campbell said.

"But they are based on our interim result, so they are quite out of date," he added. "I'm not saying they are right or wrong, but just that they're based on figures which are three months old." Campbell declined to elaborate.
Courtaulds' shares rose seven pence to 384 pence in late morning trading.
